title: Americana

metadata.credit_line: Purchased with The Marjorie and Irwin Nat Pincus Fund for Prints and Drawings

description:
By 1943, the WPA/FAP had come to an end. U.S. involvement in WWII had helped to create jobs so the federal government's assistance through WPA programs was not as necessary. Some artists and critics questioned the genuine artistic expression of art created through government programs, and Abstract Expressionism eventually dominated the art scene. Artist Stuart Davis criticized the art of Regionalists and Social Realists in a 1939 essay:

Domestic naturalism, the chicken yard, the pussy cat, the farmer's wife, the artist's model, Route 16A, natural beauties of the home town, etc., became the order of the day in painting. And on the reverse side of the popular trend toward domestic naturalism were found the more trying aspects of man's struggle with nature and society, such as the picket line, the Dust Bowl, the home-relief office, the evicted family, etc. In mural painting it was the same thing: American history-in-costume, cowboys and Indians, frontier days, picturesque industrial landscape, etc.; and on the other hand, Mexican muralism, the allegorical worker of bulging muscle and Greco-Roman profile, the fetish of fresco, etc. … What happened to the Armory Show and modern or abstract art?

Ralph Fabri's 1948 print, Americana, has it all. The U.S. Capitol dome shines in the center of the American scene, between towering smokestacks and skyscrapers of industrial cities and factories. A boxing match, the innovation of the electric lights of the theater, the Ferris wheel, and a car advertisement sit just beyond the cowboys and Indians of the frontier, and the hardworking farmer cultivating the land. Miss America, the artist's palette, books and music, frame the scene.

Fabri, born in Budapest, Hungary, immigrated to the U.S. in 1921, and became a naturalized citizen six years later. What do you think about the artist's intention in Americana? Is it a celebration of American culture and American art? Is it a criticism, or a send-up, a spoof, of the American Scene?

—Rebecca Oviedo, M.A. '16, Collections Manager/Registrar, La Salle University Art Museum
personal_notes:
Responding to the description provided on the website, I think it's a bit of both. "Americana" to Fabri was likely analagous to "chaos," for better and for worse. That's probably why the scene is littered with various anachronisms. The "Wild West" can evoke both the actual period of American expansionism but also general feelings of lawlessness and freedom. The humble lives of rural farmers in early American history working to make a living entirely their own juxtapose the looming factories and skyscrapers that utterly dominate the America yet to come over the horizon.

Perhaps he felt much of America revolves around spectacle, in many different senses. That's why a ferris wheel, boxing match, theater, and the Capitol building take center stage. The billowing cloud with rays of light beaming from it reminds me of a mushroom cloud, which isn't too unlikely considering the piece was finished in 1948. If an atom bomb isn't the most horrifying display of spectacle in all of human history, I'm frankly not sure what is. Putting it behind the Capitol building is perhaps yet another way for Fabri to suggest that American history comprises equal parts order and chaos.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Camelid Vessel

metadata.credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Alan Silverstein (class of 1970)

personal_notes:
Its asymmetrical, slighty lopsided look and eternally wall-eyed stare honestly give it a certain charm. However, as funny as it looks, the Camelid always raises a lot of questions in my mind. Who made it, and why? How often was it used as a vessel, what did it contain? The fact it's a tool, a vessel, makes it especially interesting. A simple jug or vaselike shape would have sufficied, but the creator went out of their way to make it in the shape of a camelid. Was it a certain camelid (specifically a lamine it seems) that either the creator or somebody they knew had owned? Maybe they just really liked camelids in general. We'll likely never know the full story, which is a shame but also kind of exciting. It makes me wish I could go back in time and meet whoever made it and pick their brain a little.

And that's what inspired this whole project! Picking out pieces that evoke a sense of "travel" in one way or another, be it in a metaphorical sense, a temporal sense, or a literal one. All of that makes it one of if not my favorite piece to see any time I return to the Art Museum.

-Aidan Haurin

title: The Door of Justice
personal_notes:
This piece is the most recent one in this mini-gallery, being the only one to come from the 21st Century! It's also one of the larger pieces in the special exhibition currently in the Art Museum, though it might not look like it compared to Mary or Tired Travelers.

It's one of the more metaphorical pieces; it doesn't try to take you into a scene like the nearby Mary or Gloucester Harbor. Rather like Americana to its left, The Door of Justice is more symbollic, expressing the efforts of civil rights lawyers and activists quite literally opening the door for everyday people.

Elizabeth Catlett was a American-born Mexican sculptor and graphic artist who specialized in abstract and social realist works centered around the issues and experiences of African Americans, particularly women. Being denied admission to Carnegie-Mellon on the basis of race despite her exceptional entrance exams, Catlett instead chose to attend Howard University's Art Program, where she studied design, printmaking, and drawing.

She would further refine her printmaking with linocuts after moving to Mexico in 1946 and joining the Taller de Gráfica Popular (TGP, or "Peoples Graphic Workshop") printmaking collective. Sadly, due to her civil and workers' rights activism as well as the US government alleging the TGP was a "communist front", Catlett was barred from reentering the U.S. from 1962 to 2002. However, Catlett's career thrived in Mexico, even becoming first woman to teach sculpture at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México before heading the department.

She especially valued printmaking for its affordability and accessibility, believing that art belonged not just to elites but to everyday people. She was also the first student to earn a master of fine arts degree in sculpture, the University of Iowa, with her subjects frequently exploring black womanhood through strong and maternal figures. Many of her works are still shown in public colleges, city halls, and parks, and the motifs and topics she would explore and build upon throughout all of them stemmed the iterative process of printmaking.

It's genuinely a shame this piece lacks an official description on the website, because Elizabeth's career is very extensive and very impressive. I highly recommend reading more about her when you have the chance. Who knows how many other artists in the Museum's collection have their own stories just as rich and intricate as hers?

-Aidan Haurin

title: Gloucester Harbor
personal_notes:
Woodcuts have always fanscinated me. Before the cutting even starts you probably need to sketch out the piece first, either directly onto the block or on a sheet of paper for reference. The final print's flipped horizontally, meaning you'd have to sketch it out in reverse, which sounds like a headache. Most of them only work with one color of ink for the final print, so having to convey color and texture involved varying the depth and density of your cuts into the wood. The brighter or "blank" spots counterintuitively require carving deeper into the wood than darker ones. Prints that came in color often utilized several cut blocks, each serving as a "layer" for a given color before they're pressed down in the correct order. Regardless, all of the piece is cut along the wood grain, giving woodcut prints a very distinct overall texture of line hatching from the natural grains soaking up the ink.

This piece is specifically set in Gloucester, Massachusetts, which is where the artist, Winslow Homer, had been living around the time of its creation. The subtle gradients both of the sky falling into the horizon and the countless shimmering waves alongside the crisp shading of the subjects' clothes really show a master at work. That natural hatching I mentioned here is also especially apparent. It all sells the realism of the everyday lives of the many fishers and sailors Homer probably met through the harbor, and you almost feel like you can meet them too. While La Salle's collection is almost entirely his woodcuts, he has a suprisingly extensive portfolio of watercolors and oil paintings that I also recommend looking through sometime.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Lager Beer Saloon
description:
Although Schuessele's style is academic, this ribald tavern scene with its predominantly brown palette is modeled on 17th-century Dutch genre scenes of common folk and everyday merry-making. Gas lights, with clearly visible delivery pipes, illuminate the room. The Franklin Institute awarded this painting the First Premium prize.

Schuessele was born in the Alsace region and studied lithography in Paris before settling in Philadelphia around 1848. He became Professor of Painting at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts in 1868. Schuessele established the Ladies Life Class in 1869, the first course to allow female students to study from the live model.
personal_notes:
I definitely enjoy the warmer tones and more dynamic scene at play here. Most of the pieces here lean more towards the contemplative, so I thought including something more lively would help balance out the mini-gallery. The piece has a very "you just had to be there" feel. Like Tired Travelers, it makes you wonder the little things. Who is each man; do any of them know each other and how? What's caught the attention of the two men in the center? Is the dog going to catch the newspapers slowly sliding off the table? Are the two on the far left table arguing, or is the one man retelling a story? It's just fun to pick apart small details like that in a piece.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Mary (La Sainte-Marie)

metadata.credit_line: Purchased with funds provided by Regina and Ragan Henry

description:
In this unconventional rendering of the Virgin Mary with the Christ child, Mary appears melancholy and lost in thought. The infant is almost completely covered by a shroud-like cloth, suggesting a foreshadowing of Jesus' death. Tanner paid careful attention to details studied first-hand in Jerusalem, where he first traveled in 1898. Tanner's style is academic and is distinctive for his use of luminous lighting.

The model for Mary was newlywed Tanner's Swedish-American wife. Tanner studied with Thomas Eakins at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts in the 1880s before traveling to and eventually settling in Paris, where, from 1894 on, his work appeared in the annual, juried Salon. Mary is in its original tabernacle frame with its Salon entry number, 1252, and another label noting Tanner's previous Salon medal for an earlier painting.

While it was common for American artists to travel to Paris to study art and even settle in that art-making capital, Tanner attributed his choice to remain there to the racism he encountered in the United States as an artist of mixed African-, European-, and Native-American ancestry and his ability to be judged simply by his talent in France.
personal_notes:
Mary is definitely the centerpiece of the 19th Century Gallery, and one of the Museum's more well-known pieces overall. Where most other pieces in the gallery go for vivid, lively colors and bright scenes, it goes for more faded tones and a dramatic, dour composition. Its carved frame of unpainted wood alludes to the modest yet planned-out scene before us. It's also one of the largest pieces (alongside Tired Travelers) in the Museum, which further sells the weight of the situation.

Another reason for its staying power comes from uniquely hightling the honestly dreadful position Mary is left in for most of the New Testament, despite the wondrous things her son will accomplish in time. I feel it almost parallels most depictions of the Annunciation, where the archangel Gabriel heralds the coming birth of Jesus Christ. Here he is, but where does that leave Mary? How would she know the first thing about raising a god? Does anyone know? Would anybody ever be ready to carry such a burden? And that's not even considering his eventual death, a just as if not even more mortifying thought lingering around in Mary's mind. And it is lingering in there, as shown by the very faint halo above the infant's head directly within her sight. Indeed, it's a very powerful albeit haunting piece.

-Aidan Haurin

title: More Distant Part of the Sea

metadata.medium: Color offset lithograph with embossing and collage, ed. 21/125
metadata.credit_line: Purchased with funds from William E. Kelly, Jr., '74

description:
Robert Rauschenberg used GI Bill funds to study painting at the Académie Julian in Paris. There he met Susan Weil (briefly his wife) whom he followed to Black Mountain College, where he studied under Josef Albers. The Bauhaus-inspired curriculum encouraged an openness about what constituted art, what materials might be used, and how artists might collaborate—lessons that Rauschenberg would carry throughout his career. Rauschenberg claimed to have an "insatiable curiosity" and worked in many artistic areas, including painting, sculpture, performance, technology, photography, and printmaking. He also loved to collaborate, saying, "It seems that in theater and printmaking, every individual that you add to a project will result in ten times as many new possibilities."

Rauschenberg gave two of his prints the same title, More Distant Visible Part of the Sea: one from 1979 featuring scissors, and this one from 1983 featuring umbrellas. He often included images of umbrellas, parasols, and parachutes in his art, at least as far back as the mixed media "combine" work, Charlene, from 1954. By the time he created this print, he had left the frenzy of New York City for the tranquility of Captiva Island, Florida. The serenity he found may be reflected in some of images used in this work, such as the sunset and the native flora represented.

—Thomas Blum, Ph.D.
personal_notes:
The collage being composed of specifically faded photographs feels like a stream of memories flowing back to you. Each photo being cropped give a sense of brevity or incompleteness to each memory. I find it interesting that this piece gives me a sense of the artist's "nostalgia" despite Rauschenberg only moving into Florida in his 50's and completing the piece a couple years afterward. Considering I'm writing about the piece 43 years later, they might as well be distant memories. I doubt much of the Captiva Island that Rauschenberg lived in is still there nowadays, but who knows. Maybe I could visit it one day.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Rue de La Sante and Le Val de Grace

metadata.credit_line: Purchased with funds provided by Alexis C. Manice

personal_notes:
This is one of the smaller pieces not only in this collection but in the 19th Century Gallery as well. Its frame is surprisingly deep for such a small piece. I'm not sure if this is the intended purpose, but I do think it enhances the perspectve of the street of the name that's the subject of the piece.

The painting gets its name from the street joining the 13th and 14th Arrondissements, or administrative districts, of Paris, France. The street gets its name from the nearby Sainte-Anne Hospital Center, founded in 1651. Le Val de Grace refers to a Catholic Church located in the nearby 5th Arrondissement, with its dome poking out above the treeline. The street is still in use today, and you can even recreate the picture in Google Maps.

Looking into the artist, Luigi Loir was a French painter born to housekeepers of the French royal family during their exile in Austria. Known mainly for his landscapes and ceiling paintings, he also fought in the Franco-Prussian War and illustrated for some books. Strangely, his Wikipedia page doesn't list Rue de la Sante as one of his public works, or any works in North America for that matter.

-Aidan Haurin

title: The Quest, from Don Quixote

metadata.credit_line: Gift of Dr. Richard Siebold, M.D.

description:
Salvador Dalí was a prominent Spanish artist in the Surrealist art movement. He created a Surrealist technique called 'paranoiac critical' which was applied by not only other artists but also in collaborative works with Alfred Hitchcock, Walt Disney, and the designer, Elsa Schiaparelli. Dalí was famous for his eccentric personality even compared to his fellow Surrealist artists, a group from which he was expelled a number of times. His works often incorporate themes of death, religion, and eroticism.

Surrealism was a major art movement of the early 20th century, both influenced by and interconnected with the period's politics, philosophies, and emerging psychoanalysis. Surrealist artists rejected depictions of reality and focused on unlocking the imagination through dreams and the unconscious, believing this was key to one's authentic inner voice, unweighted by the taboos of society. They often played with concepts using techniques such as 'automatism' which allowed for the artist's subconscious to take control rather than pre-planning their works. Utilizing technologies like the darkroom manipulation of photographs, Surrealists were able to create bizarre results like doubling images of themselves or making the subjects appear ethereal.

—Liana Rose D. Salazar, Class of 2022, Curatorial Intern
personal_notes:
The piece does a very good job at capturing the dynamic action of the scene from the book as abstractly as possible. I like the detail of the windmill being portrayed less as a giant like in the book but as a literal strawman, an easy target set up for Don Quixote to take down and reaffirm is delusional chivalry. You can tell Dalí was certainly playing around with "automatism" with how Don Quixote's arms are positioned on the same side of the horse, or how the rocks in the scene are haphazardly placed around. I'm not exactly sure what the blue blob in the bottom-right is meant to convey, though I always considered it to be dust clouds from the horse charging forwards.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Tired Travelers

metadata.credit_line: Gift of the Estate of Julius Bloch

description:
Julius Bloch emigrated from Germany to Philadelphia with his Jewish family in 1893. He studied at the Pennsylvania Museum School and later at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. As an immigrant he identified with working class people, many of whom suffered racial discrimination and financial difficulty. Inspired by one of his favorite artists and teachers, Thomas Eakins, Bloch became interested in Social Realism, an artistic Movement which was popular in America during the 1920s and 1930s. Over the course of his life Bloch became close friends with Benjamin Bernstein, an art patron who acquired many of his works and later donated some to the La Salle University Art Museum and other cultural institutions.

In Tired Travelers, Bloch illustrates a scene on a crowded train. The weary figures are seated in the train benches. The darkness of the windows and the way the people are dressed suggest that it is early evening and that the subjects are on their way home after a laboring day. The individuals depicted are very diverse in ethnicity, featuring an African American man and an Eastern European immigrant couple. The travelers are wearing the day's work on their faces, displaying gloomy expressions while sleeping and resting during their travel.

—Tricia Sackor, Intern, Class of 2017
personal_notes:
Alongside the Camelid Vessel, this was the other piece that inspired my initial plan for the project. It's a very calm yet contemplative piece: who are these people? What jobs do they work? Where are each of them going home to? Do they know each other outside of the bus? Maybe these are their regular seats, and after some time they get to know each other, even if only as a regular face on the bus. It gets you thinking about all these small things without being a very intricate or overwhelming piece, and I really enjoy it.

The more angular art style strongly captures each of their expressions, each worn out one way or another by the busy life in a big city. Likewise, the sheer size of the piece really drives home the weight of the day on the viewer. And yet, it also feels somewhat calming; it's a moment of rest and reprieve for each of them, which makes it almost bittersweet to take in.

-Aidan Haurin

title: Whistler by the Thames

metadata.credit_line: Gift of the Rosenbach Museum and Library

description:
One can imagine James McNeill Whistler posing for this portrait, seated on the balcony of his London flat overlooking the Thames River. But the circumstances surrounding the painting's origins are shrouded in mystery. During the 1860s and 1870s, Walter and his brother Henry Greaves were ardent students of Whistler, assisting with major commissions such as the Peacock Room. However, their relationship became estranged in the 1880s, and Walter Greaves fell into poverty, though he continued painting portraits of Whistler from memory. Following the discovery of rolls of canvases at a London pawn shop, the Goupil Gallery offered Greaves an exhibition in 1911, requiring him to sign and date many of the paintings retroactively. While the exhibition was a success, the detection that a key painting had been misdated ultimately led to a scandal, raising questions about the chronology as well as authorship of some of the paintings.

This was one of 14 paintings by Greaves that were purchased by the Rosenbach Museum co-founder Philip H. Rosenbach in 1911, which he was unable to resell due to the scandal. In 2010, with the approval of its Board of Trustees, Rosenbach Museum and Library deaccessioned all of its paintings by Greaves, auctioning off all except one that they considered the finest, which they gifted to La Salle University. It is a fascinating example of British Aestheticism, highly evocative of Whistler's work, with an interesting and enigmatic history.

This painting was conserved with support from the Irwin Nat and Marjorie M. Pincus Endowment and the Art Angels in 2011.
personal_notes:
Whistler is a painting I've used in the past for a project in my Basic Design course, so I hold a bit of personal nostalgia for it. Like Mary, it's filled with uniquely muted tones unfitting of the rest of the 19th Century Gallery. However, unlike the latter, it's quite unassuming, tucked away in one of the corners of the gallery. The way the subject, James Whistler, sits in the piece makes it feel almost like he's judging the rest of the gallery. Or maybe he's judging the viewer. Perhaps that's how Walter felt painting his mentor, or maybe how he felt struggling to get by painting from memory years down the line. Whenever he painted it, and assuming it wasn't Henry instead.

-Aidan Haurin
